title: Chunkflow investigation notes: intermittent backpressure and repro
content:
Purpose: scratchpad for reproducing intermittent SSE/chunked-response backpressure that manifests as delayed chunks, broken pipes, or full stalls under moderate concurrency. Goal is a minimal, repeatable repro and hypotheses to triage whether this is: (A) runtime producer behavior (kv-cache flushes/prefix logic), (B) proxy/edge buffering (Envoy/nginx), or (C) client-side backpressure/stream-consumption characteristics.

Context / first observation:
- Incident first seen 2026-02-10 on dedicated pool 'd-nyc-1' for model variant r/infer-v2-q4.
- Symptoms: client sees long pauses between token-chunks (~100–800ms) even though server logs show steady token generation. Sometimes connection resets with \"broken pipe\" or \"upstream prematurely closed connection\".
- Affected paths are streaming chat endpoints and sync generator endpoints with prefix KV reads.

Environment notes:
- Fronting: Envoy (edge) -> API gateway -> runtime pool (go-based runtime + python model shim).
- Observed headers: Transfer-Encoding: chunked; no Content-Length. Response sometimes contains gzip; we set transfer-enc chunked + gzip combo in a couple of tests.
- Runtime uses continuous-batching, writes tokens to net.Conn from a token emitter goroutine. Writes are small (avg 120–240 bytes).

Commands tried (clients that reproduce behavior):
1) Raw curl without buffering: curl -v --no-buffer -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' "https://api.redwood/test/stream"
   - Good for seeing immediate chunk flow, but some pauses are still visible.

2) Curl with explicit HTTP/1.1 and keepalive: curl -v --http1.1 --no-buffer "https://api.redwood/test/stream"

3) Python requests streaming:
   python -c "import requests
url='https://api.redwood/test/stream'
r=requests.get(url, stream=True, headers={'Accept':'text/event-stream'})
for i,line in enumerate(r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True)):
    if line: print('L',i,line)
    if i>100: break"
   - Observed: sometimes iter_lines yields larger aggregated chunks (lines concatenated) — suggests proxy buffered multiple chunks.

4) Node fetch / readable stream experiment (client backpressure test):
   node snippet that reads response.body.getReader() slowly (sleep 150ms between reads). Under these conditions, server write returns false earlier (checked by instrumenting runtime) and we see internal write slowdowns.

5) wrk2 load test to create many concurrent readers and small writes:
   wrk -t8 -c200 -d30s --latency -s scripts/streaming.lua https://api.redwood/test/stream
   - Increased frequency of broken pipe and connection resets under mid-level concurrency.

Server-side quick repro scripts used locally:
- Go: minimal chunked server that writes small tokens and flushes:
  package main
  import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
  )
  func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fl, _ := w.(http.Flusher)
    for i:=0;i<200;i++ {
      w.Write([]byte(fmt.Sprintf("%d: token\\n", i)))
      fl.Flush()
      time.Sleep(40*time.Millisecond)
    }
  }
- Node: express + res.write + res.flush using compression off and res.flushHeaders(); used to simulate small-chunk bursts and verify proxy differences.

Proxy experiments and configs checked:
- Envoy: checked proxy_buffer_limit / max_downstream_connection_attempts / drain windows. No custom buffer limits set, default 1MB.
- nginx: proxy_buffering on/off toggles reduce aggregation in some runs (turning off buffering reduces aggregated chunks).
- Hypothesis: fronting proxy sometimes buffers multiple small writes from upstream before sending to downstream, causing observed pauses.

Error snippets captured from production logs:
- \"write tcp 10.0.3.12:443->10.0.5.9:52784: write: connection reset by peer\"
- \"http: response.WriteHeader on hijacked connection\"
- \"rpc: EOF while flushing\"
- Client side: \"Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers\" from net/http
- Envoy: \"upstream response length: insufficient\" (partial logs)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Proxy-level buffering + gzip/content-negotiation: compression + small chunk sizes cause proxy to aggregate until threshold (min_size) or until flush event. When aggregate hits a threshold we see a burst of data, otherwise client perceives pauses.
2) Runtime's write path ignoring backpressure signal: in Go, w.Write may not block as expected when underlying TCP send buffer is full because runtime uses intermediate buffers or goroutine scheduler masks slowdowns. Need to watch net.Conn Write return errors and check if write returns n < len(buf).
3) Client reading behavior: some clients (requests.iter_lines, curl buffering, browser fetch reader) will coalesce or delay yielding partial chunks; client libraries can mask server-side micro-chunk behavior.
4) KV cache or prefix logic stalls: if runtime waits on KV read that stalls for tens of ms when cache miss cascades, chunk stream halts then resumes. But server logs show token generation continues — less likely.

Instrumentation / checks to add:
- Add per-write timing metric at runtime: timestamp before write, after write, and whether Write returned full length or partial or error. Emit as event to logs (sampling 1/1000 requests).
- Add socket-level tcp_info stats (snd_cwnd, rtt) on write errors to correlate NIC-level backpressure.
- Modify runtime to set TCP_NODELAY explicitly and re-run.
- Enable Envoy downsteam_flush_packets_on_close or similar flags to ensure immediate flush.

Minimal reproducible experiment to run locally (steps):
1) Start local Envoy with default config that matches production (one listener, route to upstream on 127.0.0.1:8080).
2) Run the Go minimal server above on :8080.
3) Run client: curl --no-buffer http://localhost:10000/stream -v and wrk tests to simulate concurrency.
4) Toggle envoy config: set http_connection_manager.downstream_flush_policy to IMMEDIATE vs AUTO and observe chunk latencies.

Concrete repro commands copy-paste:
- Start server (Go):
  go run ./cmd/minichunk/server.go &
- Start envoy (local):
  docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/envoy.yaml:/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml -p 10000:10000 envoyproxy/envoy:v1.29.0
- Client tests:
  curl -v --no-buffer http://localhost:10000/stream
  node slow-reader.js  # reads with 150ms pause between reads
  wrk -t4 -c100 -d20s -s ./scripts/streaming.lua http://localhost:10000/stream

Observed differences that mattered:
- nginx with proxy_buffering off reduced aggregated bursts.
- Envoy downstream_flush_policy: IMMEDIATE also reduced pause amplitude.
- Disabling gzip removed batch aggregation in several runs — suggests compression/deflate buffering interaction.

Quick notes on mitigation ideas:
- Force flush semantics at the runtime layer (call Flush() at writer every N bytes) and ensure TCP_NODELAY is set.
- Avoid per-token gzip/compression; negotiate to disable for SSE endpoints.
- Add an explicit chunk delimiter and occasionally send a \"heartbeat chunk\" (1 byte) every 50ms to keep proxies/clients moving.

Next steps (action items):
- [ ] Add sampled per-write timing logs in runtime and ship to staging (Evan).
- [ ] Stand up local Envoy with production-ish config and run automated wrk script to replicate (Marta).
- [ ] Try disabling gzip on runtime for SSE endpoints and retest with same client set (Jamal).
- [ ] If reproduces, prepare small PR that toggles downstream_flush_policy in envoy template and/or sets TCP_NODELAY for runtime sockets.

Open questions to answer:
- Is this only happening for requests that go through certain route policies (model variants pinned to different hosts)?
- Do dedicated pools with different NIC drivers exhibit different behavior? (intel vs aws-ena)
- Are there any intermediate CDN caches that could be re-buffering?

Raw traces & snippets appended here for quick copy: (examples)
- netcat chunked producer: printf 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\\r\\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\\r\\n\\r\\n5\\r\\nhello\\r\\n0\\r\\n\\r\\n' | nc -l 8080
- curl client to test: curl -v --http1.1 --no-buffer http://localhost:8080/

Final note: keep this doc minimal and iterative. Goal is to converge on whether the aggregator (proxy) or writer (runtime) is the root cause. If tests consistently show proxy toggles fix the symptom, prioritize configuration change and add a targeted instrumentation PR to confirm in staging before production rollout.

Breadcrumbs: created quick gist of the Go server at https://gist.github.com/evan/mini-chunk-server (private) for rapid iteration.

-- Evan
